F2.Q1: Dressed stone slabs — pale sandy flagstones, rectangular, laid in staggered courses with dark recessed joints between them.
F2.Q1_WHY:
The joint lattice is unambiguous. Measuring the dark rows across the lit floor (x 310–750) puts horizontal joints at y ≈ 16, 42, 80, 112, 144, 208, 250 — a course roughly every 32px, half a game tile. Vertical joints at x ≈ 334, 364, 384, 434, 491, 515, 619, 631 — irregular spacing, so slabs vary in width but not height. Courses are offset between rows (running bond). The face colour where the lamp is strongest, around (392,88), sits at luminance ~215 with a warm cream cast; in the dim east it drops to ~40 but keeps the same hue. Cut stone, not poured, not tile, not earth.

---
F2.Q2:
South, down the corridor at x 500–564, y 275–470.

And I have to be straight with you: **nothing about the ground made me pick it.** I picked it off the walls. It's the only opening in the image that reads as a bounded passage rather than an edge of the lit area, so it's the only one that looks like a decision. The floor inside that corridor — I zoomed it at (470,260)–(600,460) — is the same slab, the same joint pitch, the same cracks, the same value as the room floor at the same lamp distance. If you erased the magenta blocks either side of it I could not tell you that corridor was a corridor.

---
F2.Q3:
It's been cracked and splattered, and nothing else. It has damage but no history.

There's a network of long thin black lines running across the whole visible floor, and about a dozen dark splat-shaped stains. What's absent is everything that comes from use: no polish, no hollowing, no darkened track, no grime banked into the corners, no chips at the slab edges, no debris, no patch, no repair. For a floor in an underworld in continuous heavy use since before the records, with a company of orcs on it for four hundred years, it reads as if it were laid, cracked, stained, and then never touched.
F2.Q3_WHY:
- The cracks (e.g. (400,198)–(440,218), (325,50)–(365,70), the long arc through (350,210)–(500,260)) run *straight over the joints* as though the floor were one continuous plate. A slab floor fractures along its joints and stops at slab edges. These don't — they cross the mortar lines without deviating or terminating.
- Their shape is smooth, curving, branching meander. That's a vine or a cable, not a fracture. Fractures are angular and they stop.
- The splats — the clearest one at (440,150)–(490,195) — are a round clump with scattered outlier pixels around it, a spray pattern. They sit on the slab as an overlay and are not conformed to it.
- I measured slab interiors for any wear-derived tonal variation and found none in the lit area (see Q8B).

---
F2.Q4:
Two things, and both are the same problem.

**The splats.** The same round spray blob recurs at roughly (350,25), (455,158), (515,170), (385,220), (540,225), (600,235), (155,110), (205,125), and a couple more in the east murk. They aren't pixel-identical — I template-matched the one at (455,158) and the best non-self hit was 0.55 — but they're the same idea at the same size, ten-plus times in one screen, evenly scattered. Once I saw the third one I started counting them instead of looking at the room.

**The hatch fields.** In the dimmer east, whole slab-sized patches are filled with a 45° diagonal scratch pattern — same angle, same spacing, snapped to a 32px sub-lattice. I template-matched the patch at (635,120) and got hits at 0.65–0.75 at (611,88), (577,88), (559,120), (595,184), (431,56), (439,120), (503,88), (485,18), (529,120), (651,184), (431,18). Every hit lands on the 32px grid. It's one stamp, placed twelve-plus times.

The cracks also pull harder than they should. In the lit area a crack pixel sits at ~0.15–0.21 of the local floor value — near black against cream. They are the loudest element in the frame, louder than the figure's silhouette.

---
F2.Q5:
**Repeated.** The hatch evidence above is decisive: a small set of detail stamps placed on a 32px lattice, correlating 0.65–0.75 across a dozen positions. The splats are the same story with more variation. The slab lattice itself has a fixed 32px course height everywhere with no variation across the whole floor.

The crack overlay is the one part that argues the other way — it's drawn continuously across tile boundaries and doesn't respect the 64px grid, which is real authorship. But it's the only layer that does, and it's laid on top of a stamped floor rather than emerging from it.

---
F2.Q6:
**YES.** It's coherent, it's readable, the lighting sells it, and nothing in it looks broken.

Merely competent, or genuinely good? **Merely competent.** It clears the bar and stops. Nothing in the surface is doing work that a stamped-decal pass and a crack overlay couldn't do, and there is no place on this floor where I can point and say someone made a decision about *that spot*.

---
F2.Q7:
Legible at 1:1:
- The joint lattice — slab shapes, course offsets.
- The black crack lines. Very legible, they dominate.
- The dark splats, as soft smudges — I can tell something is there, not what.
- Overall warm tan, and the lamp gradient.

That's the entire list. **The slab faces are blank at 1:1.** Flat cream, no grain, no speckle, no tone. Under the lamp the face is one value with a lighting ramp across it.

Only visible after magnifying:
- A sparse 4px dither on the faces — perhaps three or four blocks per slab, one value step darker. Invisible at native size.
- The 45° hatch fields.
- Vertical tally-like scratch marks and horizontal dash marks in the west band.
- Ring/circle shapes in the west and far east.
- Per-slab base-value variation — individual stones reading lighter or darker than neighbours. This exists in the dim east but not in the lit centre.

That last group is real work that nobody will ever see. It's all hunting, not seeing.
F2.Q7_WHY:
Checked at 1:1, no magnification: the full frame; then native crops (308,0)–(750,276) and (490,270)–(570,470). In both I could resolve joints, cracks and smudges, nothing on the faces.
Had to magnify: (378,84)–(414,106) at 12× to find the 4px dither; (600,60)–(750,200) at 5× with brightness ×3 to find the hatch fields and rings; (140,60)–(310,150) at 5× ×3 to find the tally and dash marks; (440,150)–(490,195) at 8× ×2.2 to resolve a splat's actual shape.

---
F2.Q8:
It reads as **one age everywhere: laid a long time ago, cracked, and then frozen.** Call it a century or two — old enough to have fractured, not old enough to have been walked.

The problem is that it reads *uniformly* one age, and that's what makes it wrong for this place. There is no part of this floor that is older than another part, no part repaired, no part re-laid, no part beaten down. A floor in continuous use since before the records would be a patchwork of ages — and would show it as differential wear, replaced slabs, hollows.
F2.Q8_WHY:
- Crack density measured as dark-feature fraction: upper-left room (312,8)–(436,140) = 0.282, centre around the figure (372,110)–(500,240) = 0.236, lower-left (312,140)–(436,270) = 0.215. Comparable regions at comparable lamp levels, comparable damage. No region is more beaten than another.
- Slab geometry is identical throughout: 32px course pitch at (310,0)–(750,275) and equally at (500,275)–(564,470). No slab is a different size, a different colour, or set at a different depth — nothing has been replaced.
- No debris anywhere. Corners at (312,250)–(360,275) and (700,10)–(750,60) are as clean as the centre.

---
F2.Q8B:
**NO BASIS.**

I tried to get this from the surface and the surface refused. What I did: sampled 768 low-variance 6×6 patches across the lit floor, skipping joints and cracks, binned them by distance from the lamp at (408,172), and took each patch's residual against its distance-bin median — i.e. what's left after removing the lamp falloff. Residual std came back at 41.5, which looked promising until I mapped it. The darkest residuals cluster at (338,190)–(378,238) and the brightest at (442,182)–(482,238) and (330,118)–(338,150). Those are exactly the shadow wedge running down-left of the figure and the bright wedge opposite it. It's the light cone's *shape*, not the floor. Once you account for the lamp, the residual is zero.

Crack density is flat across the lit region (0.215–0.282 across three comparable areas). Splat placement is even scatter, not clustered on any line. Slab base value is uniform in the lit centre. Joint darkness is constant.
F2.Q8B_WHY:
Nothing in the surface put a mark anywhere, because I could not find a mark to place. Value: all lighting. Colour: one hue everywhere. Texture: the faces are blank. Joints: identical width and value across the whole floor. Debris: none. Confidence that there is no wear signal here: **high.** I checked for it four different ways and every apparent signal resolved to the lamp.

---
F2.Q9:
**The ground told me nothing.** I read the route off the walls.

Standing at (408,172) with light reaching roughly to x=620 east and y=260 south before it gives up, I can see maybe six metres of floor in every direction, and there is no direction in which that floor is different from any other direction. No track, no polish, no scuff line, no grime channel, no smoothing of the joints along any axis. If you told me this figure was standing on a daily route I would have no way to confirm it, and no way to tell you which of the four ways it runs.
F2.Q9_WHY:
Regions along the candidate south route: (500,180)–(564,275) at the corridor mouth, then (500,275)–(564,400) inside it. Regions I'd have rejected: (330,100)–(400,200) to the west, (560,80)–(680,200) to the east, (350,0)–(500,80) to the north.
What's different about the ground between them: **nothing that isn't the lamp.** Same 32px course pitch, same joint value, same crack contrast ratio (0.21 at (400,198) in the lit centre, 0.16 at (325,50) to the north-west — both just tracking local brightness), same blank faces, same splat frequency. I compared the corridor mouth against the room's dead centre directly and they are the same floor.

---
F2.Q10:
Judged from the ground alone: **they all look the same.**

Four ways out of the lit region — north across the top edge at (310,0)–(750,0), east off the right edge at (750,0)–(750,275), west into the dim band at (120,30)–(180,145), and south down the corridor at (500,275)–(564,470). I examined the floor immediately in front of each. Same slab, same joint pitch, same crack density, same blank faces, same absence of debris. Not one of these thresholds is worn more than another, and none of them is worn at all. There is no most-used door here and no abandoned one.

---
F2.CULL:
Every slab reads identical — blank faces at 1:1, zero wear, detail only from repeated stamps and cracks.

- Put grain on the slab faces that survives at 1:1 — currently the face at (378,84)–(414,106) is flat cream and only shows three dither pixels at 12×.
- Cut the crack overlay's contrast (it's at 0.15–0.21 of local floor value) and make cracks terminate at joints instead of running smooth arcs across them.
- Break the 32px stamp lattice — the hatch at (635,120) repeats at eleven other positions all snapped to the same grid.
- Add wear differentiation the surface can carry: darkened, joint-smoothed ground through the corridor mouth at (500,180)–(564,340) and the room's centre line, grime and debris banked in the corners at (312,250) and (700,10).

F1.Q1: Cut stone paving — rectangular slabs, pale sand colour, laid in running bond with dark recessed joints. That is as far as I can honestly go: I can name the *format* confidently and the *material* only by assumption. Nothing on the faces tells me stone rather than concrete, plaster screed, or fired clay.
F1.Q1_WHY:
The joint lattice at x 310–750, y 0–272 is unmistakable — courses ~60px tall, slabs of varying width (full, half, quarter) offset course to course, joints 3–4px and consistently darker. But the slab *faces* under the lamp (x 374–502, y 196–272 magnified 7×) are a single flat cream fill with at most a one-pixel lighter top edge. No grain, no bedding, no pitting, no tonal split between slabs. I'm reading the mortar, not the stone.

---
F1.Q2:
South, down the corridor at x 502–566. **Nothing about the ground influenced that.** The walls chose it for me — it's the only single-tile passage in frame and it reads as a route by geometry alone. The paving inside that corridor mouth (x 502–566, y 272–336) is identical in tone, joint width and surface to the paving I'd be leaving behind at x 374–500, y 140–260. If I'd been shown the ground alone with the walls stripped out, I'd have had no reason to prefer it over west or east.

---
F1.Q3: It has cracked and nothing else. A branching hairline fracture network runs across it — but the slabs are square-edged, fully seated, uniformly coloured, unchipped on their faces, uncovered, unstained, and completely undisturbed. Nothing has been dropped on it, spilled on it, swept across it, dragged over it, repaired into it, or worn off it. It reads as a floor that has been sitting still.
F1.Q3_WHY:
The cracks are real and well done — a continuous 1px staircase line enters at ~(430,0), runs down to ~(400,140), branches, and one arm crosses eight or nine separate slabs to ~(620,265). It crosses joints without breaking, which means it's an overlay drawn on top of the tile grid rather than per-tile decoration. That's the only damage. Against it: joint width is constant everywhere I sampled; no slab is lower, tilted, or lipped against its neighbour; the floor region x 310–750, y 0–272 contains 3,928 unique colours but they all sit in a **single hue band, 20°–60°** — there is not one differently-coloured thing on this floor. No repair timber, no rope, no pin, no rust, no soot, no dust drift at the wall base. For a place where a garrison patches everything with salvage, the floor has been patched zero times.

---
F1.Q4:
Yes, three things, and only one of them is a compliment.

1. **The hard-edged diagonal dither bands** at x 320–392, y 150–270 and x 490–560, y 200–272. Stepped 45° light shafts rendered as chunky ordered dither. At 1:1 they read as texture on the floor, not as light, and they are the loudest thing on the walkable surface — louder than anything actually on the stone. My eye goes there first every time and it's an artefact of the lighting pass.
2. **The 45° hatch stamp.** Once magnified and brightened, the same cluster of 4–6 parallel diagonal scratch lines appears on dozens of slabs across x 600–750, y 0–260 and x 130–300, y 25–145. Same angle, same spacing, same count. It's one motif dealt out repeatedly.
3. **The blankness of the four slabs around the figure** — x 374–500, y 140–260. My eye keeps going back because it expects to find something there and there is nothing.

---
F1.Q5:
**Made** — for the room. But the corridor fails it outright, and I want that on the record rather than buried.

The room's joint layout does not repeat: I cross-correlated every 64px floor cell against every other and the best genuine floor pair scores 0.64. Slab widths vary, course offsets vary, and the crack network is authored across the grid. That is a made surface.

The corridor is not. Cells at x 502–566 for y = 272, 336, 400, 464, 528 correlate 0.45–0.77 against each other *in raw pixels, through a steep lighting falloff* — and a 20px patch at (502,304) matches (502,368) at **r = 0.995**. It's one 64px tile stacked five times, same joint skeleton, same chip mark. The one stretch of floor the level pushes you down is the one stretch that's a photocopy.

---
F1.Q6:
**YES.**

Merely competent. The lighting is handsome, the crack authoring is genuinely better than average, and nothing here is broken. But it is not good. Good would mean the floor carried information — where people go, how long it's been there, what was done to it. This floor is a well-lit paving diagram.

---
F1.Q7:
**The faces are blank at 1:1.** Excluding the joints and the crack overlay as instructed, there is nothing legible on the face of a single slab anywhere in this image at played size.

Legible at 1:1: the joint lattice, the crack lines, the diagonal dither bands. All three are excluded or are lighting.
Only on magnification: the 45° hatch clusters; short horizontal ruled/tally lines; heavy black cross and "T" glyphs; small incised mark clusters. Some of it is nice work — the tally-like glyphs around (220–250, 88–105) suit a ledger-underworld exactly. None of it survives to the screen.
F1.Q7_WHY:
- Checked at **1:1** — x 374–502, y 196–272 (brightest paving, directly beside the lamp); x 330–378, y 190–212; x 392–440, y 216–240; x 456–504, y 152–176. A joint-free 30×16 window at (389,216) has a total luminance range of 53, and virtually all of that is the lamp's own falloff across 30px, not surface. High-frequency content inside joint-free bright faces is dither noise, not form.
- Had to **magnify and brighten** — x 560–750, y 0–270 at 5× and ×9 gain; x 110–320, y 0–150 at 5× and ×6 gain; x 490–580, y 270–600 at ×7. The far-east floor at x 600–740, y 20–250 sits at mean luminance **14/255, 95th percentile 19**. That is black on a phone. Every authored mark on this floor is in there.

The detail and the light are in complementary places. Where you can see, there is nothing; where there is something, you cannot see.

---
F1.Q8:
It reads as **laid within living memory and never walked on** — call it a decade or two, in a building that has since settled. That is flatly at odds with the fiction, which wants ground older than the records.

It reads as **one age everywhere.** I can find no part that is older or newer than any other — not the corridor, not the alcove, not the room.
F1.Q8_WHY:
From x 374–502, y 140–272 and x 502–566, y 272–336, magnified. Slab corners are sharp right angles; edges are straight with no rounding, no cupping, no lipping of one slab above its neighbour; joint width is uniform across the whole visible floor, including at the corridor mouth where the funnelling geometry should have ground the joints wide and shallow. Old paving loses its arrises first — these have all of theirs. The only ageing evidence is the crack network (x 430,0 → 620,265), and cracks are settlement, which happens to new floors too. There is no *use* evidence anywhere.

---
F1.Q8B:
**NO BASIS.**

I cannot mark it. The floor surface carries no traffic signal I can read.
F1.Q8B_WHY:
I flat-field-normalised the image (divide by a 45px blur) to strip the lamp out, masked off joints and cracks, and measured mean face brightness in 48px blocks across the whole lit room, x 310–750, y 0–272. Values run 0.77 to 1.65 — a wide spread — but the spread maps **exactly onto the diagonal shadow shafts**, not onto any path: the lows (0.77, 0.85, 0.87 at x 454–598, y 0–48) sit precisely where the occlusion band falls, and the highs sit in open light. Remove the lighting and the faces are uniform. Beyond that: joint width is constant, so no ground-down grout; there is no debris anywhere to be absent from a path; and the floor is monochrome within one hue band, so there is no polish, no darkening, no dust-tone shift to read.

Confidence: **high** that the signal genuinely isn't there, rather than that I failed to find it. I checked value, hue, saturation, joint width, and high-frequency texture separately, and all four are flat.

---
F1.Q9:
No. The ground told me nothing. I read the route off the walls.

The light reaches roughly 230px from the figure — comfortably far enough to show me a route if one were drawn. Within that radius I can see south to about y 340, east to about x 640, west to about x 300, north to the top edge. In every one of those directions the paving is the same paving.
F1.Q9_WHY:
Along my nominal route — x 502–566, y 272–340 (corridor mouth, still lit at mean luminance 78) and the approach to it at x 440–520, y 200–270. Rejected — x 330–420, y 90–200 (west of the figure) and x 560–650, y 60–200 (east). **What is different about the ground between them: nothing.** Same slab colour, same joint width, same blank faces, same absence of debris. The corridor cells are marginally *cleaner* than the room if anything — no cracks reach into x 502–566 at all — which if I took it literally would argue the corridor is the *less* used ground, the opposite of what the geometry says.

---
F1.Q10:
**They all look the same.**

Four ways out are visible: the south corridor (mouth at x 502–566, y ~278); the western alcove/passage (mouth at x ~300, y 25–150); the east edge (x 750, y 0–270); and the north edge (y 0, x 300–750). Judging only from the ground in front of each, I can't rank them.

There *is* a visible difference in slab marking between them — the west alcove approach (x 250–320, y 60–145) and the east approach (x 690–750, y 100–260) carry hatch and ruled marks that the corridor mouth entirely lacks. But that isn't traffic. It's tile-variant assignment: the marked variants are scattered through the dim outer ring and the blank variants happen to sit under the lamp, and the pattern doesn't organise around any opening. The corridor mouth — which the level layout makes the single busiest square metre in frame — is the *blankest* ground in the image.

---
